title: NAT Gateways, Public IPv4 & IPv6 Costs
summary: Outbound internet access patterns and the hourly and per-GB charges behind them.
tldr: A **NAT gateway** bills per hour **and per GB processed**. The biggest saving is to keep AWS-service traffic off it: **gateway endpoints** for S3 and DynamoDB (free), interface endpoints for other services such as ECR.
Every **public IPv4 address** is billed hourly since February 2024, whether attached, idle or auto-assigned. Put servers in private subnets behind a load balancer and release unused Elastic IPs.
For IPv6, an **egress-only internet gateway** gives outbound-only access with no hourly charge and no public IPv4 address.
One NAT gateway per AZ is the high-availability design. For dev or test that accepts losing egress when one AZ fails, a single NAT gateway is the cheapest.

keyFacts.text: Charge for each public IPv4 address, in use or idle (about $3.60 a month each). Applies to EC2, load balancers, NAT gateways and unattached Elastic IPs.
S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints have no hourly or per-GB charge. Same-Region S3 traffic through them skips NAT processing fees.
Private image pulls need `ecr.api` and `ecr.dkr` interface endpoints, plus the S3 **gateway** endpoint because image layers are stored in S3.
An egress-only internet gateway has no hourly charge; you pay normal data transfer out. It works for IPv6 only.

traps: An S3 **interface** endpoint charges hourly and per GB; for in-VPC S3 traffic the free **gateway** endpoint is cheaper.
An egress-only internet gateway handles IPv6 only; it cannot replace a NAT gateway for IPv4 traffic.
Swapping auto-assigned public IPs for Elastic IPs doesn't cut cost; both are public IPv4 addresses billed hourly.
Unattached Elastic IPs still cost money; release them.
A Graviton NAT instance saves little and adds operational work; endpoints remove the per-GB charge instead.

sections.heading: Regional NAT gateway (new in late 2025)
sections.body: AWS added a **regional availability mode** for NAT gateways (November 2025). One regional NAT gateway spans the AZs where your workloads run and doesn't need a public subnet, so you no longer manage one gateway and route table per AZ. Exam questions written before then still expect the classic answer: **one zonal NAT gateway per AZ** for resilience.
